summary:
Every spacecraft has a story. Some are still sending signals, while others have gone silent. Our project, *Abandoned But Not Forgotten*, aims to keep their stories alive through an interactive website.

We built this website using *React and Vite* for the frontend, *Python and FastAPI* for the backend, and *GitHub and Vercel* for collaboration, version control and deployment. We used *3D visualisation* to create an interactive Solar System and spacecraft experiences. We also integrated *OpenRouter AI* with a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system to create ASTRO, an AI assistant.

For research, we referred to trusted space resources, including *NASA mission archives, NASA/JPL records, the National Space Science Data Center (NSSDCA), the Apollo Surface Journal, and official ISRO information about the Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan).*

The journey was not easy. We faced several challenges, including API errors, AI model failures, backend and frontend integration, 3D feature development, GitHub collaboration, deployment issues and repeated debugging. We tested different solutions, fixed errors and improved the website step by step.

This project taught us teamwork, problem-solving, research and practical development. Most importantly, we learned that even when a spacecraft goes silent, its contribution to science should never be forgotten.
details:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive web experience that honors the spacecraft we’ve left behind on other worlds. Visitors explore a 3D solar system, choose a planet, and see the hardware humanity has left there. On 3D Mars and Moon globes, they can find documented landing sites marked with verified coordinates. They can also walk through a floating 3D museum of Mars rovers, lunar landers, descent stages, probes and orbiters. Each spacecraft has its own artifact page. The Spirit rover’s page lets you inspect it in 3D, see a parts breakdown, read its “Last Signal,” and follow a synchronized timeline. We also built an 11-stage, first-person story of Spirit’s journey, with animated visuals, audio narration, and scrubbing and hotspots. An AI copilot called ASTRO answers questions in context, backed by a Python FastAPI RAG system and an offline NASA knowledge engine, so it still works if the backend is down.

The project makes space history easy to approach for people with no technical background. It teaches real engineering and mission details while also making people feel something for these machines. We hope it keeps the legacy of retired missions alive and inspires curiosity about exploration.

We built it with TypeScript and Vite on the frontend, Python and FastAPI on the backend, and Python scripts to generate textures. We used Lovable for development, Vitest for testing, and Vercel for deployment. It runs in a browser, so no special hardware is needed.

What makes it creative is that it treats dead spacecraft as characters rather than data. The “Last Signal” idea, the first-person storytelling, and the gallery-style museum give each mission an emotional ending.

We considered accuracy (verified coordinates and NASA-grounded answers), reliability (the offline fallback), and usability (responsive design, cross-navigation and narration). We also built it in phases, with a full test suite and a clean production build.
